props.title: Things to Come
props.initialSlug: Epic vision of civilization's fall and rebirth

sections.content: Things to Come (1936) stands as H.G. Wells' ambitious vision of humanity's future, crafted during the anxious pre-WWII period. The film's striking Art Deco aesthetics and modernist architecture influenced science fiction for decades, directly inspiring later works like 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and Logan's Run (1976). What's remarkable is how Wells accurately predicted WWII starting in 1940 (only off by one year), and the film's depiction of aerial bombardment proved horrifyingly prescient. The movie spans a century of human development, from civilization's collapse through to a technological renaissance.

movies.title: When Worlds Collide
movies.slug: George Pal's influential disaster film about humanity building spacecraft to escape Earth

sections.content: The film's three-act structure mirrors humanity's cycle of destruction and rebirth. The first act's devastating "Wandering Sickness" plague eerily foreshadows later pandemic films like The Andromeda Strain (1971) and 12 Monkeys (1995). The second act's tribal warlord society predicted the post-apocalyptic genre that would later flourish with films like Mad Max (1979). The final act's gleaming technological utopia, with its massive video screens and space program, established visual tropes still used in contemporary sci-fi.

Director William Cameron Menzies, primarily known as a production designer, brought Wells' vision to life through groundbreaking special effects and massive sets. The film's influence extends beyond science fiction - its innovative montage sequences and epic scope influenced directors like Stanley Kubrick and Ridley Scott. The movie's warnings about technological warfare and societal collapse remain relevant, while its optimistic view of scientific progress offers hope. SUBHEAD: Prophetic Elements and Modern Relevance

sections.content: Wells' screenplay demonstrates remarkable foresight about technological developments. The film predicted technologies like flat-screen displays, wireless communication, and space travel decades before they became reality. Modern films like Minority Report (2002) and Children of Men (2006) echo Things to Come's mix of dystopian warning and technological speculation. The film's depiction of society rebuilding after catastrophe influenced later works like The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) and Planet of the Apes (1968).
